transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-05-04
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood Solutions), Nina Patel (Head of ML, LyricAI), Samir Rao (CTO), Emily Wong (Platform Eng), Marcus Li (SRE)

Optional auto-summary: quick intake on per-token economics and deploy modes; customer leans private/dedicated for IP + latency; exploring pilot budget ~ $25k/month equivalent; wants short prompt optimizations (batching less effective) - explore KV/prefix caching and lightweight quantized models.

Topics: pricing per-token and per-request, batching vs cache for short prompts, dedicated/reserved capacity and burst, private V P C options and SSO/KMS, pilot scope and success criteria.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Maya from Redwood Inference, i'm the AE on this account. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Nina: hi this is Nina, head of ML at LyricAI.
[00:08] Samir: Samir here, CTO.
[00:10] Emily: emily, platform eng.
[00:12] Marcus: Marcus, SRE.
[00:14] Diego: diego from redwood, i'm the solutions engineer, i'll run through some of the latency/cost tradeoffs.
[00:18] Maya: cool, goal for today — understand your workload and budget, and then outline hosted vs dedicate vs private options and where we think you'll land.
[00:26] Nina: perfect, quick context — LyricAI does on-demand lyric gen for user-submitted prompts, so latency needs to be interactive under 400ms p50 ideally, p95 under 900ms. Lots of requests are very short — like 8-40 tokens input, generation ~ 40-120 tokens. We also have a heavy daylight qps pattern, big spikes after product releases.
[00:45] Samir: and IP — the prompts sometimes include proprietary artist seeds and customer billing data, so we need either a private deployment or strict data residency and KMS controls.
[00:55] Maya: got it. Diego, do you want to walk through per-token and caching options?
[01:00] Diego: sure. So, two levers for unit economics — batching and caching, and also model choice / quantization. For short prompt workloads, batching is trickier because batching adds queuing latency, so at low latency SLOs you can't always batch heavily. Caching — prefix or KV cache — is very effective for repeated prefixes, for instance system prompts or reused artist prompts. That reduces per-token compute.
[01:28] Emily: our traffic has a lot of repeated templates — users often start with the same scaffold. Would prefix caching help in that case?
[01:34] Diego: yes, prefix caching is probably your best win. If 30-40% of requests share a common initial prompt, then k v cache gives you the ability to serve part of the sequence from cache and only compute the remainder. We saw effective savings of 20-50% in similar workloads. (note: some words may be garbled, e.g., 'kv' shown as 'k v' in some exports).
[01:55] Nina: what's the expected per-token delta between hosted and dedicated? our rough budget is about $25k/month initially.
[02:02] Maya: depends on model and QPS. Hosted API has a standard per-token pricing (we'll send the sheet), dedicated is reserved GPU capacity which converts to a lower effective per-token cost at steady usage but you pay for reserved capacity. For your bursty profile dedicated with burst/overprovisioning or a hybrid mix often makes sense.
[02:22] Diego: to give numbers — for a 13B quantized model on hosted, you might see $0.0009 per token generation cost ballpark (this is illustrative), dedicated with good utilization we can get down to $0.0004-0.0006 per token because of pooling and continuous batching. But again, with short prompts you may not realize full batching gains. Caching pulls costs down further.
[02:47] Samir: those hosted numbers seem high given our volume expectations. Are there ways to lower hosted egress cost?
[02:53] Diego: hosted pricing is simpler but we can carve out a pilot pricing arrangement for committed usage. Also model selection matters — smaller model families with tuning can hit your quality bar for less cost; Redwood has a model catalog and we can recommend a few that match lyric generation quality.
[03:09] Nina: what's the latency tradeoff of using a smaller quantized model vs a larger one with more compute but better quality?
[03:16] Diego: smaller quantized models reduce latency per token and cost, but might hallucinate or produce lower-quality lyrics. We recommend A/B testing prompt sets — Redwood Optimize can generate prompt-level quality regressions and tie to cost.
[03:30] Emily: technical question — if we go private (on-prem or V P C), how much extra ops overhead do we need? 
[03:36] Priya: hi — from solutions, private deployment includes a control plane we still manage and a customer-managed data plane in your VPC. There's an on-prem bundle for air-gapped. Typical setup time 4-8 weeks depending on networking and KMS. We'll provide automation and runbooks; your SRE team still needs to manage upgrades if you choose full on-prem.
[03:56] Marcus: 4-8 weeks is big — we have a product launch 8 weeks out, ideally pilot before then. Will hosted pilot keep us compliant enough?
[04:03] Maya: we often run hosted pilots with strict data handling — options include disabling logs retention, bringing your own key (BYOK), and per-customer project isolation. For full compliance you might prefer dedicated or private, but we can scope a hosted pilot that satisfies some requirements short-term.
[04:20] Samir: what's the SLA and uptime on dedicated pools? we can't tolerate long retries during peak.
[04:26] Diego: dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and predictable throughput. We also support autoscaling policies and burst capacity patterns. For critical routes we configure fallbacks to a cheaper model or region automatically to avoid complete outages — graceful degradation.
[04:42] Nina: can you explain how fallback affects cost? if we fall back to a smaller model during peak, will that spike our billing?
[04:49] Diego: fallback reduces latency but may change quality. Cost-wise, smaller models cost less per-token; fallback could actually reduce spend during peak compared to overprovisioning large GPUs. But if fallback causes additional retry logic from the app, that can increase calls. Need to design routes carefully.
[05:05] Emily: our prompts often include sensitive metadata — SSO/SAML and audit logs are requirements for enterprise. Do you integrate with major IdPs?
[05:12] Priya: yes, Redwood supports SSO/SAML, RBAC, and audit logs; for private we can integrate customer KMS/HSM for keys. We'll share the security pack.
[05:21] Samir: pricing question — do you charge per-request or per-token for embeddings vs generation?
[05:27] Maya: generation is per-token; embeddings are per-embedding unit (we'll have unit definitions in the sheet). For LyricAI the generation cost will be dominant.
[05:34] Nina: what's the typical pilot success criteria — we want both latency under 400ms p50 and acceptable quality for 90% of prompts, while staying within $25k/month projected.
[05:43] Maya: that sounds reasonable as pilot KPIs. Proposed pilot: 4 weeks, run on hosted with reserved burst capacity, use a tuned 7-13B quantized model, enable KV prefix caching, track p50/p95 and cost per 1k generations, tie quality to a small prompt set. If those metrics hit targets we scope dedicated/private for launch.
[06:04] Samir: budget wise — $25k/month — can you illustrate the TCO for hosted vs dedicated? 
[06:10] Maya: yes — hosted pilot -> pay-as-you-go with pilot discount; dedicated -> monthly reserved GPU commitment (we'll model using your qps profile). We'll send a spreadsheet comparing both with assumptions: qps by hour, prompt length distribution, cache hit rate.
[06:25] Emily: on caching — what cache hit rate assumptions are realistic? we think 35% of users reuse scaffolds, but there are many unique prompts.
[06:33] Diego: 30-40% is plausible and gives material savings. But for long tail unique prompts you get little caching. We can also talk about application-side techniques like prompt templating to increase cacheability.
[06:47] Nina: are there any hidden costs — inference orchestration, tracing hooks, console usage?
[06:52] Maya: observability is included but long-term storage/advanced retention is an add-on. Also enterprise integrations (extra audit retention, custom SLAs) are priced as add-ons. We'll outline those in the security and pricing docs.
[07:03] Marcus: rollouts — can we do canary with automatic rollback? our dev cycle needs that.
[07:08] Diego: yes, Redwood supports canary deploys and automatic fallbacks to previous model version or alternative model. That helps mitigate regressions.
[07:16] Nina: one more — batching: since our prompts are short, is there sense in investing time in batching strategies?
[07:21] Diego: batching helps at high concurrency when latency SLO accepts small additional queueing. For strict <400ms p50, batching window must be tiny. So likely less benefit. Focus on caching and model choice first. Batching helps more for longer sequences and high steady QPS.
[07:36] Samir: ok, next steps?
[07:38] Maya: recap and next steps — we'll send pilot pricing and TCO spreadsheet, security pack, and Diego will run a micro-benchmark plan. You (Emily) will share traffic profile. Let's set the technical canary planning call.
[07:50] Nina: sounds good.
[07:52] Marcus: thanks everyone.
